describes: A closed, positive list of base-form (bare-infinitive) verbs the six requires_verb_complement modal_lexemes.json entries ('shall be entitled to', 'are entitled to', 'shall be empowered to', 'shall be authorised to', 'shall be authorized to', 'shall have the power to') accept as the first word of their complement. The match is only accepted when that first word is, case-insensitively, EXACTLY one of these entries (no lemmatisation, no suffix stripping): an infinitive complement in English is always the bare verb form, so 'paid' (a past participle: 'paid annual leave') and 'receiving' (a gerund: 'receiving compensation') are never in this list and are correctly rejected by construction, not by a separate check. A word outside this list is NOT treated as a wrong reading of this cue; for five of the six entries the parser falls back to the next (shorter) ranked modal_lexemes alternative at the same token position (deontic.prose_grammar._match_longest_filtered), exactly as it would if these five phrases were not published at all, and that fallback itself then abstains on its own pre-existing terms (the remaining text opens on 'be', a state_action_prefixes entry, so action resolves to ACTION_IMPLICIT). 'shall have the power to' is the one exception: its own entry carries 'abstain_if_no_verb_complement': true, because its fallback (the bare lexeme 'shall') does NOT abstain on its own — the remaining text opens on 'have', which is not itself a state_action_prefixes entry (only the two-word 'have been'/'has been' are), so a failed verb check here falls through all the way to an accepted O/duty reading unless the match is refused outright and the whole sentence abstains instead (NO_MODAL, nothing else in the sentence to try). 'noun_markers' (['of', 'for']) is a second, additive check over the word RIGHT AFTER the matched verb: several of these verbs are also common nouns that take 'of'/'for' where the verb reading never does ('transfer OF the data', 'charge OF the case', 'record OF the processing', 'claim OF compensation', 'share OF the profits', 'address FOR service', 'act OF', 'request OF', 'use OF the facilities', 'control OF the data', 'process OF law', 'order OF the court') — a match whose second word is 'of' or 'for' is rejected even though the first word is a listed verb, because the second word is exactly the signature of the NOUN reading, not the verb one ('use THE data', 'order THE controller to comply', 'transfer personal data' all keep working: their second word is never 'of'/'for'). This also covers the degenerate case where 'of' is the very last word published in the complement (the sentence ends right after it): the check is on literal word identity, not on what (if anything) follows. 'verb_specific_noun_markers' adds a per-verb extra marker where 'of'/'for' alone would miss a genuine homograph: 'access' the VERB is monotransitive in English ('access THE FILE', never 'access TO the file'), while 'access' the NOUN regularly takes 'to' ('a right of access TO the file'); 'to' right after 'access' is therefore ALSO rejected for that one verb only ('entitled to access TO the file' is a noun reading; 'entitled to access THEIR PERSONAL DATA' and 'empowered to request access to the premises' — where 'access' is the OBJECT of a different governing verb, 'request', not the word this check examines — both keep working). Derivation: every verb below is attested in the EU digital-law corpus — GDPR (2016/679), the AI Act (2024/1689), the DSA (2022/2065), NIS2 (2022/2555), the ePrivacy Directive (2002/58), the Data Act, the Data Governance Act, the Trade Secrets Directive, the Cyber Resilience Act, DORA, eIDAS, the Product Liability Directive, the CDSM Directive, and national implementing acts filed alongside them — as either (a) the verb immediately following one of 'entitled to'/'empowered to'/'authorised to'/'authorized to'/'have the power to'/'has the power to' in the corpus text itself (the direct search `grep -ohiE "(entitled to|empowered to|authorised to|authorized to|have the power to|has the power to) [a-zA-Z]+"` over the corpus), or (b) a comparable bare-infinitive 'to <verb>' construction attested elsewhere in the same corpus (`grep -ohiE "to <verb> [a-z]+"`) for a verb this family of cues plausibly governs elsewhere in EU/national digital-law text but that happened not to collocate with one of the six exact cue phrases in this corpus snapshot (issue, terminate, engage, intervene, notify, comply — e.g. 'to issue guidance', 'to terminate the agreement', 'to engage in', 'to intervene in automated decision-making', 'to notify the authority', 'to comply with Article 15(1)'). A verb the corpus does not attest in either shape is deliberately left OUT rather than guessed at (a false negative here is an abstention, never a wrong P/privilege or P/power reading): 'audit'/'inspect'/'investigate' are examples left out on purpose even though they are plausible regulatory powers, so 'shall have the power to audit the controller'/'... to inspect the premises' correctly abstain rather than guess at a reading this corpus snapshot does not attest for these exact cues. The direct search's own non-verb hits were excluded, each for a stated reason, confirming the method also surfaces the false positives a cruder filter would miss: 'compensation', 'information', 'fees' are plain nouns; 'such', 'a', 'an', 'the', 'fair', 'further', 'legal', 'equal', 'paid' are determiners/adjectives/a past participle leading a noun phrase, never the verb itself; 'temporarily' is an adverb leading a verb ('to temporarily ... suspend'), not itself a verb — left out rather than resolved by skipping it, so 'shall have the power to temporarily ... suspend the testing' also correctly abstains for the same reason 'audit'/'inspect' do. 'reopen' ('... entitled to reopen the decision ...') IS a genuine, directly attested verb and is included below.
